rewritten_text:
Colonel Grangerford was a gentleman, you understand. A gentleman through and through, and his whole family was the same. He came from good stock, as people say, and that counts for as much in a man as in a horse, according to the Widow Douglas. Nobody ever questioned that she belonged to our town’s finest aristocracy. Dad always said so too, though he had about as much breeding himself as a catfish. Colonel Grangerford was very tall and slender, with skin that was pale but slightly dark, without a touch of red anywhere. Every morning he shaved his whole narrow face clean. His lips and nostrils were extremely thin, his nose high, his eyebrows heavy, and his eyes so black and so deeply set that they seemed to look out at you from caves. He had a high forehead, and straight black hair hanging down to his shoulders. His hands were long and thin. Every single day he wore a fresh shirt and a complete linen suit so white it hurt your eyes to look at him; on Sundays he put on a blue tailcoat with brass buttons. He carried a mahogany cane topped with silver. There was nothing silly about him, nothing at all, and he never raised his voice. He was as kind as anyone could be—you could sense it, which made you trust him. Now and then he smiled, and you were glad to see it. But when he drew himself up straight as a flagpole and lightning started flashing beneath those eyebrows, you wanted to climb a tree before finding out what was wrong. He never needed to tell anyone to behave. People always remembered their manners when he was there. They all liked having him around, too; he was nearly always sunshine—I mean he made things feel like good weather. When he turned into a thundercloud it got terribly dark for half a minute, and that was enough. Nothing would go wrong again for a week.

When he and his wife came downstairs in the morning, everyone in the family stood up from their chairs and wished them good morning, and nobody sat again until they were seated. Then Tom and Bob went over to the sideboard, where the decanter stood, mixed a glass of bitters, and brought it to him. He held it and waited while they mixed their own. Then they bowed and said, “Our respects to you, sir and madam.” The old couple gave the slightest little bow and thanked them, and all three men drank. Bob and Tom added a spoonful of water to the sugar and the little bit of whiskey or apple brandy left at the bottom of their glasses and handed them to Buck and me. We drank to the old people as well.

Every properly made boy reaches a point in life when he desperately wants to go out and dig for buried treasure. One day this urge seized Tom. He went looking for Joe Harper but couldn’t find him. Next he tried Ben Rogers, who had gone fishing. Before long he ran into Huck Finn the Red-Handed. Huck would do. Tom led him somewhere private and explained his idea in confidence. Huck was willing. He was always ready to join any scheme that promised fun and needed no money, since he had an inconvenient surplus of the kind of time that isn’t money. “Where are we digging?” Huck asked.

“Oh, just about anywhere.”

“What, is it hidden everywhere?”

“Of course it isn’t. People hide it in very particular places, Huck—sometimes on islands, sometimes in rotten chests under the end of a dead tree’s branch, exactly where its shadow falls at midnight. Mostly, though, it’s beneath the floors of haunted houses.”

“Who hides it?”

“Robbers, obviously. Who did you think? Sunday-school directors?”

“I don’t know. If I had it, I wouldn’t hide it. I’d spend it and enjoy myself.”

“So would I. But that isn’t how robbers operate. They always bury it and leave it.”

“Don’t they ever come back for it?”

“No. They mean to, but they usually forget the landmarks or else they die. Anyway, it sits there a long time getting rusty. Eventually someone finds an old yellow piece of paper explaining how to find the landmarks. It takes about a week to decipher because it’s mostly symbols and hieroglyphics.”

“Hiero—what?”

“Hieroglyphics. Pictures and things that don’t seem to mean anything.”

“Have you got one of those papers, Tom?”

“No.”

“Well, how will you find the landmarks, then?”

“I don’t need landmarks. They always bury it under a haunted house, or on an island, or under a dead tree with one branch sticking out. We’ve searched a bit on Jackson’s Island and can try again sometime. There’s the old haunted house up Still-House branch, and there are loads of trees with dead branches. Loads of them.”

“Is there treasure under every one?”

“What a thing to ask! No!”

“Then how do you know which to try?”

“We try them all!”

“But Tom, that’ll take the whole summer.”

“So what? Suppose you find a brass pot holding a hundred dollars, all gray and rusty, or a rotting chest filled with diamonds. How about that?”

Huck’s eyes lit up.

“That’s fantastic. More than good enough for me. Just give me the hundred dollars. I don’t need any diamonds.”

When my tears had ceased, reason and recollection came back to me, and I began more calmly to consider what had occurred and what conduct now became me. Only a few hours had elapsed, yet an immense change had overtaken my existence—the ordinary labour of years had been accomplished since morning. My father was dead to me, and for an instant I felt as though he lay white-haired in his coffin, while I, my youth departed and age approaching, mourned his death at its appointed season. Yet this was false: I was still young, alas, much too young, and to others he was not dead. But I, most wretched, must never again look upon him or address him. I must flee him more eagerly than I would my bitterest enemy; neither in lonely places nor amid cities might I see him more. This thought stole my breath with anguish, and fastening upon my imagination prevented me for a time from pursuing any connected reflection. Henceforward, I thought, I would inhabit the bleakest solitude. I would withdraw to the Continent and take the veil, not from religious feeling, since I was no Catholic, but to be shut away from the world for ever. There I might find a solitude in which to weep, beyond the reach of living voices.

But my father—my dear and utterly miserable father? Would he perish? Could he never conquer the violent passion that now ruled him without pity? Might he not, after many, many years, when age had extinguished the burning feelings he suffered now, become my father once again? This thought smoothed my forehead, and I felt—and wept to feel—a smile, half sorrowful, loosen the expression of pain upon my lips. I ventured to entertain happier expectations of my future. Years must intervene, but hope would lend them wings and carry them swiftly by; or though they dragged, they would nevertheless pass, and my father was not lost to me eternally. Let him endure another sixteen years of lonely wandering. Let him pour out his wild lamentations once again to the boundless forests and mighty waterfalls of a foreign land. Let him face anew terrible perils and hardships that subdued the soul. Let the southern sun again scorch his passion-wasted cheeks, and cold nocturnal rains descend upon him and chill his blood.

To such a life, unhappy father, I condemn thee! Go! Spend thy days among savages and thy nights beneath the arch of heaven! Let thy limbs grow weary and thy heart grow cold, until all youth within thee is extinguished!
